Redefining Vectors and Matrices

When you hear the word "vector," your mind probably jumps straight to physics or calculus. You have likely been trained to think of a vector as a quantity with both magnitude and direction—like acceleration, velocity, or displacement. For example, a velocity vector in three-dimensional space might look like this: \begin{equation} \tag{1} \vec{v} = \begin{pmatrix} v_x \\ v_y \\ v_z \end{pmatrix} \end{equation} where v_x, v_y, and v_z represent the velocity components along the x, y, and z axes.

But in this class, we are going to look at vectors from a slightly different angle. A vector is really just a convenient way for us to organize a set or collection of numbers. You can write them in a row-wise fashion or a column-wise fashion. For our purposes, we do not need to think about physical direction in space. Instead, we can use a vector to hold our human and zombie populations at a given hour: \begin{equation} \tag{2} \vec{p} = \begin{pmatrix} h \\ z \end{pmatrix} \end{equation} where h is the number of humans and z is the number of zombies. It might feel a little weird at first to think of populations as a vector, but if you can accept that a vector is just a handy box for organizing numbers, you are in good shape.

So, if that is a vector, what on Earth is a matrix? You might have heard it called an "array," but if that is too fancy a word, let’s just call it a box. A matrix is a box of numbers or parameters. More specifically, it is a box of numbers that does stuff to a vector. In mathematical terms, a matrix operates on a vector. You feed a vector into this box, the matrix transforms it, and it spits out a brand new vector. \begin{equation} \tag{3} \text{[Matrix]} \times \text{[Vector]} = \text{[New Vector]} \end{equation}

In our zombie model, what does the "brand new vector" represent practically compared to the vector we fed into the matrix?

The input vector holds the human and zombie populations at the start of a given hour. The matrix acts as the rules of the outbreak, transforming those numbers based on our infection and cure rates. The new output vector gives us the updated, resulting populations for the next hour!

Building the Matrix Equation

Let’s make this concrete by returning to our zombie apocalypse scenario. We want to find out how many humans and zombies there will be at the current hour (let’s call it hour n) based on the populations from the previous hour (hour n-1).

Recall the conversion rates from our previous discussion:

  • a_{z \leftarrow h}: The fraction of humans who turn into zombies each hour.

  • a_{h \leftarrow z}: The fraction of zombies who are cured (turned back into humans) each hour.

On Monday, we set a_{z \leftarrow h} = 0.2 (20% of humans are lost to zombies) and a_{h \leftarrow z} = 0.1 (10% of zombies are cured). This gave us a system of two equations to track the populations: \begin{align} h_n &= 0.8 h_{n-1} + 0.1 z_{n-1} \tag{4} \\ z_n &= 0.2 h_{n-1} + 0.9 z_{n-1} \tag{5} \end{align} The 0.8 comes from the fact that humans retain 100\% - 20\% = 80\% of their population naturally, and the 0.9 comes from zombies retaining 100\% - 10\% = 90\% of theirs.

We can generalize this system using our parameters instead of specific numbers: \begin{align} h_n &= (1 - a_{z \leftarrow h}) h_{n-1} + a_{h \leftarrow z} z_{n-1} \tag{6} \\ z_n &= a_{z \leftarrow h} h_{n-1} + (1 - a_{h \leftarrow z}) z_{n-1} \tag{7} \end{align}

Now, here is the magic of linear algebra. We can take these two separate equations and rewrite them in a much more aesthetically pleasing way as a single matrix equation. We package our updated populations into a new vector on the left, our previous populations into an input vector on the right, and our coefficients into a 2 \times 2 matrix in the middle: \begin{equation} \tag{8} \begin{pmatrix} h_n \\ z_n \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 - a_{z \leftarrow h} & a_{h \leftarrow z} \\ a_{z \leftarrow h} & 1 - a_{h \leftarrow z} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} h_{n-1} \\ z_{n-1} \end{pmatrix} \end{equation}

Plugging in our specific numbers from Monday, our matrix equation becomes: \begin{equation} \tag{9} \begin{pmatrix} h_n \\ z_n \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.8 & 0.1 \\ 0.2 & 0.9 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} h_{n-1} \\ z_{n-1} \end{pmatrix} \end{equation} Why do we bother doing this? Because computers love matrices and vectors. If you have a complicated system with many interacting groups, you can punch the entire situation into a computer as a single matrix equation. The computer can then instantly calculate useful properties, like eigenvalues and eigenvectors, which we will explore next time.

The Paper-Tearing Method for Matrix Multiplication

If you are new to linear algebra, it might not be obvious how to multiply a 2 \times 2 matrix by a 2D vector. To make it tangible, let’s use a physical analogy.

Imagine you have a generic matrix with elements a, b, c, d and a vector with elements x, y: \begin{equation} \tag{10} \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} = \text{?} \end{equation} Mentally (or physically, if you have scratch paper) rip the vector \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} away from the matrix. Turn it horizontally so it reads (x, y). Now, lay this horizontal vector over the top row of the matrix, (a, b). Multiply the elements that line up and add them together: a \cdot x + b \cdot y. This becomes the top element of your new vector.

Next, slide your horizontal vector (x, y) down to the bottom row of the matrix, (c, d). Multiply the aligned elements and add them: c \cdot x + d \cdot y. This becomes the bottom element. \begin{equation} \tag{11} \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} ax + by \\ cx + dy \end{pmatrix} \end{equation} A common misconception is that the result is another 2 \times 2 matrix because the expressions look large. But remember, ax + by evaluates to a single number, and cx + dy evaluates to a single number. The result is just a new 2D vector.

If you multiply a 2 \times 2 matrix by a 2D vector, why doesn’t the operation create a new 2 \times 2 matrix?

Because of how the math lines up! When you lay the vector across a row of the matrix, you multiply the matching pairs and add them together into one single number. Doing this for both rows gives you two numbers stacked on top of each other, which is just a 2D vector.

Let’s try it with some boring, arbitrary numbers just to practice the mechanics: \begin{equation} \tag{12} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1(5) + 2(6) \\ 3(5) + 4(6) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 + 12 \\ 15 + 24 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 17 \\ 39 \end{pmatrix} \end{equation}

Tracking the Outbreak Hour by Hour

Now let’s put our matrix to work and track the zombie outbreak. At Hour 0, we started with 15 humans and 0 zombies. Our initial population vector is: \begin{equation} \tag{13} \vec{p}_0 = \begin{pmatrix} 15 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \end{equation}

To find the populations at Hour 1, we feed \vec{p}_0 into our matrix: \begin{equation} \tag{14} \vec{p}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 0.8 & 0.1 \\ 0.2 & 0.9 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 15 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.8(15) + 0.1(0) \\ 0.2(15) + 0.9(0) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 12 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} \end{equation} At Hour 1, we have 12 humans and 3 zombies.

To find Hour 2, we take our new vector \vec{p}_1 and feed it back into the same matrix (since the conversion rates have not changed): \begin{equation} \tag{15} \vec{p}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0.8 & 0.1 \\ 0.2 & 0.9 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 12 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.8(12) + 0.1(3) \\ 0.2(12) + 0.9(3) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 9.6 + 0.3 \\ 2.4 + 2.7 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 9.9 \\ 5.1 \end{pmatrix} \end{equation} At Hour 2, we have 9.9 humans and 5.1 zombies.

Let’s do one more step for Hour 3: \begin{equation} \tag{16} \vec{p}_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 0.8 & 0.1 \\ 0.2 & 0.9 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 9.9 \\ 5.1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.8(9.9) + 0.1(5.1) \\ 0.2(9.9) + 0.9(5.1) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 7.92 + 0.51 \\ 1.98 + 4.59 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 8.43 \\ 6.57 \end{pmatrix} \end{equation}

Visualizing the Transformation

Even though we are not talking about physical direction in space, we can still sketch these population vectors on a graph. Let the x-axis represent the human population (h) and the y-axis represent the zombie population (z). The length of the arrow represents the magnitude of the populations, and the direction shows the ratio of humans to zombies.

When you look at the graph, you can visually see what the matrix is doing to the vector. Each hour, the matrix rotates the arrow toward the zombie axis and shortens its overall length. The total population h + z always stays at 15, but because the diagonal distance is shorter than the sum of the components, the physical length of the arrow decreases. If we were to run this calculation for a very large number of hours (N = 1000), the vector would eventually settle at a steady state of 5 humans and 10 zombies.

If the total population is always 15, why does the physical length of the arrow on our graph get shorter as time goes on?

Think about the geometry of a right triangle! The total population is just the direct sum of the x and y components (h + z). However, the length of the arrow is the hypotenuse, calculated using the Pythagorean theorem (\sqrt{h^2 + z^2}). As the population shifts from being concentrated on one axis to a mix of both, that diagonal distance shrinks even though the sum of the components stays constant at 15.
